transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. Well, I guess what brings me in is... I just, I feel like I can’t settle in my own body anymore. It's really hard to explain, but it's like this constant, uncomfortable energy. 

I'll be at home—I'm not working right now, so I'm supposed to be managing the house—and I try to sit down to do things that really shouldn't be that big of a deal. But especially when I’m supposed to sit quietly and handle paperwork, or if I'm trying to sit down and go over shared household plans, I just... I can't do it. I physically feel like I need to jump out of my skin. I end up shifting around in my chair, or I keep finding excuses to get up, like suddenly needing a glass of water or needing to check the mail, but it's really because sitting there trying to focus on those plans or forms feels almost impossible. 

I mean, I got my bachelor's degree years ago, so I used to be able to sit and do things, but lately, it's just this overwhelming feeling of not being able to just *be still*. And it's causing friction because the paperwork just piles up on the kitchen counter, and the household plans get put off, and then I feel incredibly guilty about it. But every single time I force myself to sit quietly and look at it, that terrible restlessness is just right there again, and I just don't know how to turn it off...

You mentioned you used to be able to sit and focus on things years ago when you were in school. When did you first start noticing this restlessness and difficulty sitting still—was it always like this for you, even as a child, or is this something more recent?

Well, it's funny you ask that, because when I said I could focus in college, I think I just meant I had figured out ways to mask it or work around it, because if I really sit down and think about it... oh wow, no, it definitely goes way, way back. 

Looking back, this was absolutely already a part of me in elementary school. I actually found this old box of report cards in my mom's basement a few years ago, and reading through them was like a lightbulb going off. I was totally that girl with the horribly messy desk—I mean, it was an absolute disaster zone in there, just crumpled up papers and broken crayons and things I was supposed to take home but never did. I was constantly losing things. I was famous in my house for forgotten permission slips. My mom would get so frustrated because she’d find them at the bottom of my backpack three weeks after the field trip happened, just completely crushed. 

And the teachers... oh my goodness, the notes from my teachers were always the same. Every single year, they would write these little comments in the margins saying that I talked out of turn, or that I was being disruptive because I would just blurt things out instead of raising my hand. And they constantly pointed out that I seemed completely unable to stay seated. I was always the kid getting up to sharpen a pencil that didn't need sharpening, or asking to go to the bathroom just so I could walk down the hall, or just sort of hovering next to my chair instead of sitting in it. So I guess the feeling of needing to jump out of my skin has always been there, really. It’s just that when you're eight, they just tell you to sit down and stop talking, and now that I'm an adult, it's my kitchen counter that looks like that messy desk, and I don't have a teacher telling me to sit still, I just have this... this awful internal pressure. But yeah, it's definitely not a new thing, it was right there in second and third grade...

When you're trying to focus on something like reading or paperwork, do you find that your mind wanders or that you have trouble keeping your attention on the task itself, or is it more that your body just won't stay still even though your mind might be willing?

Well, that's the thing, it's really both, but the mind wandering is... it's honestly just as bad as the physical fidgeting, maybe worse, because it feels so out of my control. Like, I’ll tell myself, "Okay, you're going to sit down right now and read this planning email from your sister about the family reunion," or, "You're going to read one chapter of this book for the book club you joined because you thought it would be good for you to get out of the house." And I’ll sit down, and for the first minute or two, I'm doing it. I'm looking at the words, I'm reading the sentences. I start out completely fine. 

But then, it's like a switch flips in my brain, and I don't even realize it's happening at first. I'll be staring right at the screen or the page, and my eyes are moving across the words, so physically I'm doing the action of reading. But my mind is completely gone. I'm thinking about whether I left the porch light on, or remembering a conversation I had three days ago and wondering if I said the wrong thing, or I'm suddenly obsessing over the fact that the dog needs a bath. And then I sort of snap back to reality and realize I've been staring at the exact same paragraph for five minutes, and absolutely none of it went in. Not a single word. 

It’s so incredibly frustrating because I *want* to read it. My mind is willing when I sit down, but it just won't stay there. I have to read the same email three or four times just to understand what time we're supposed to meet for lunch. And with books, I end up having to backtrack pages and pages because I realize I have no idea what just happened in the story. It's like my brain just takes a detour without asking my permission, and it happens every single time I try to focus on something like that. It's exhausting, honestly, just trying to keep my own thoughts on a leash.

Beyond the difficulty with sitting still and focusing on paperwork or reading, do you find that this restlessness and trouble concentrating affects other areas of your life—like your relationships, your ability to do household chores, or activities you actually enjoy doing?

Oh, absolutely. It... it really bleeds into everything. It’s not just the paperwork, it’s honestly my whole life right now, and it breaks my heart to say it, but the fallout has been that people at home just... they can’t reliably count on me. And my husband tries to be understanding, but I see the look on his face when he comes home and the house is a disaster. Like, I’ll start the laundry, right? I'll gather all the baskets, bring them downstairs, but on the way, I notice the hallway mirror is smudged, so I go to the kitchen to get the glass cleaner. But then I see the trash is full, so I pull that out to take to the garage, and then I notice the dog's water bowl is empty so I start scrubbing that out... and three hours later, the laundry is still just sitting in a massive pile in the middle of the stairs and the trash bag is blocking the back door. He just sighs, you know? Because I *am* trying hard. I'm trying so incredibly hard to manage the house like I'm supposed to.

And it’s really spilled over into the things I actually like doing, too. Since I'm not working, I used to be really active in a few volunteer circles—the local PTA, and this community garden project. I loved it, I really did. But I’ve actually had to step back from some of those responsibilities recently because... well, because I keep letting things fall through. I was supposed to organize the spring planting schedule for the garden, which just meant calling a few nurseries and making a simple list for the group. But every time I tried to sit down and do it, I'd get that awful jumpy feeling, or my mind would wander off completely, and I ended up missing the deadline to order the discounted seeds. I let the whole committee down. 

I had sticky notes everywhere, I put reminders in my phone, I even bought a special planner, but it didn't matter. I just kept dropping the ball despite trying my absolute hardest to keep it all together. It got so embarrassing that I finally just emailed the volunteer board and told them I needed to take a step back for personal reasons. But the real reason is just that I know they can't rely on me right now, and I couldn't bear the guilt of messing up their plans again. It’s an awful feeling, knowing you want to help, and you have the time to help, but you just can't trust yourself to actually follow through on any of it...

When you're doing something you really enjoy—like watching a movie, spending time with friends, or doing an activity where you don't have to sit still—do you still feel that same restless, jumpy energy, or does it mainly happen when you're trying to focus on tasks like paperwork?

Oh, I wish it was just the paperwork, I really do. Because you'd think, right? You'd think if it's something relaxing, something I actually *want* to do, my body would just let me enjoy it. But no, it absolutely happens then, too, and it is so incredibly frustrating. 

Like, just the other night, for example. My husband and I, we were trying to just have a nice, quiet evening. He works such long hours, and I just wanted us to have a peaceful night where we sit on the couch together. I had my book—the one for that book club I mentioned earlier—and he was reading the news on his tablet. I even made chamomile tea to try and set this really calm, cozy mood, and I brought out this soft chenille blanket my mother-in-law knitted for us a few years ago. I *want* that quiet evening reading beside my husband so badly. I really do crave that downtime. 

But I sit down, and it’s like my body just completely rejects the quiet. Within five minutes, I'm shifting all my weight around, trying to get comfortable. Then I remember something the neighbor said earlier that day about the trash pickup schedule, so I just blurt it out and start talking, completely breaking the silence. And then I start humming—which I don't even realize I'm doing half the time, it's just this unconscious noise I make, but my husband definitely notices. And then I decide my tea needs a little bit of honey, so I get up to go to the kitchen. Then I sit back down, but my foot is tapping against the coffee table. 

And it just keeps going like that. I end up talking, humming, getting up for all these tiny, insignificant little things, or just generally making enough noise that it completely stops being peaceful. It completely ruins the vibe. And my husband will just kind of sigh and put his tablet down, and I feel terrible because I'm the one who suggested the quiet reading night in the first place! It's like I physically cannot just exist in a quiet, relaxing space, even when it's exactly what I want to be doing, because that jumpy energy just has to get out somehow.

Beyond the restlessness and trouble focusing, do you find yourself making impulsive decisions or saying things without thinking them through first? For example, do you ever spend money suddenly without planning, interrupt people in conversations, or make snap decisions that you later regret?

Oh, the interrupting... yes. It is so embarrassing because I really, truly pride myself on being a good listener. Or at least I want to be. I care a lot about being respectful to people, and my parents always taught me how important it is to let others speak, but... I still jump into my husband’s conversations all the time. Or I will just completely finish people’s thoughts for them. 

It happened just this past weekend, actually. My husband was on the phone with his brother, and they were talking about this new car his brother is thinking of buying. Some kind of hybrid, I think, or maybe a small SUV. Anyway, my husband was trying to explain something about the dealership they visited, and I just kept chiming in from the kitchen while I was making lunch. I kept telling him to ask about the warranty, or reminding him to mention the tire package, and he finally had to cover the receiver and give me this exhausted look. 

And it is not just with him, it happens with my friends, too. If someone is telling a story and they pause for even half a second to find a word, I just blurt out the word for them. I think I am being helpful in the moment, or maybe my brain just moves too fast, but the response just comes out before I’ve made myself wait. 

I really do want to let them finish their own sentences. I know exactly how rude it looks. But the words are already out in the air before my brain even registers that I should have kept my mouth shut. It makes me feel so awful because people probably think I just do not care about what they have to say, or that I think my thoughts are more important, but I do care! I really do! It is just this sudden impulse, and I cannot seem to catch it in time, no matter how much I tell myself beforehand to just bite my tongue and listen.

When you were a child in elementary school, beyond the fidgeting and talking out of turn, did teachers or your parents ever describe you as hyperactive or overly energetic? For example, did they say you were always on the go, or that you seemed to have excessive energy compared to other kids your age?

Oh, definitely. Looking back, I mean, it’s so clear to me now that this was already very much a part of me way back in elementary school. It wasn't just a phase or me being a typical kid, you know? 

I was always—and I mean *always*—the girl with the absolute messiest desk in the entire classroom. It was like a black hole in there. I remember in fourth grade, my teacher actually had me stay inside during recess to clean it out because I couldn't find a single assignment, and it was just this avalanche of crumpled up papers, broken crayons, and, of course, all those forgotten permission slips. Oh, the permission slips! My mother used to get so incredibly frustrated with me because I’d almost miss out on field trips to the zoo or the science museum because the slip was just buried at the absolute bottom of my backpack for three weeks, completely crushed under my library books. 

And as for the energy... yes, absolutely. My parents actually kept this whole file folder of my old report cards and progress reports in the hall closet, and it was always the exact same story year after year. They were constantly getting notes from teachers saying that I talked out of turn—which, I guess, goes right along with what I was just saying about interrupting my husband, right? It’s like I haven't changed at all! But the teachers would also specifically write that I seemed completely unable to stay seated. 

They definitely saw me as overly energetic. Like I had a motor inside me that just wouldn't shut off. I would get up to sharpen my pencil five times during a short spelling test, or I'd be kneeling on my chair instead of sitting on it, or I'd just be wandering over to the reading corner when we were supposed to be doing our math worksheets at our desks. My mom used to say I was like a little tornado moving through the house, and the teachers definitely felt that in the classroom, too. It’s actually kind of sad to think about now, because I really wanted to be the good, quiet student who sat perfectly still with her hands folded, but I just... I couldn't keep my body in that little plastic chair. I just had to be moving, and I guess everyone around me definitely noticed it.

When you think back to your childhood—say, between ages 5 and 12—was this restlessness and difficulty concentrating present pretty much all the time during those years, or were there periods where it seemed to go away or get better?

Hmm, ages five to twelve... let me really think about that. Because, you know, childhood memory can be such a funny thing, especially when you're trying to look back that far and pinpoint exactly how you felt year by year. But honestly? No, I really don't think there was ever a time where it just... stopped. Or even got better. 

I can't remember any sort of magical phase where I suddenly calmed down or could just sit and focus like a normal kid. It feels like it was just this constant, uninterrupted hum in the background of my entire childhood. Like, if I think about kindergarten—I had Mrs. Gable, she was so sweet—I was the one who couldn't stay on my carpet square during storytime without rolling around or bothering the kid next to me. And then you fast forward to, say, third grade, and it was the exact same story, just with harder worksheets and a bigger desk to make a mess of. 

I remember my parents actually thought that maybe I just needed to burn off steam, you know? Like maybe if they just tired me out, the restlessness would go away and I'd be able to pay attention. So they put me in absolutely everything. I did gymnastics, I did swimming lessons at the YMCA, I was in Girl Scouts... oh, I was a Brownie, and we had these meetings in the basement of the Methodist church down the street from our house. And even there, when we were supposed to be sitting at these long folding tables working on our little crafts or listening to the troop leader explain a badge, I was still the one squirming out of my seat, losing my glue stick, completely zoning out while she was giving instructions. 

And it wasn't just during the school year, either! You'd think, oh, it's summer vacation, she doesn't have to concentrate on spelling tests, so maybe the restlessness will take a break. But no, I was just driving my mom crazy at home instead of driving the teachers crazy at school. I'd be pacing around the kitchen, starting a puzzle and abandoning it five minutes later, just constantly bouncing from one thing to the next. 

So, I mean, to answer your question... no, I really don't recall any periods where it faded away. It was just pretty much all the time, every single year, straight through elementary school and right on into middle school. I was just always, always like that.
When you got to middle school and high school, do you remember if the restlessness and trouble focusing got any better, or did it stay pretty much the same as it had been in elementary school?

Middle school... wow, that is a whole different era to unpack. You know, going from having just one main teacher in elementary school to suddenly having a different teacher for every single subject... it was such a massive shock to the system. I remember we had these tall, skinny metal lockers, and mine was just... well, it was exactly like my fourth-grade desk, just vertical. I would just shove my winter coat and my gym clothes and all my loose, uncategorized papers in there until the door literally wouldn't latch anymore and the janitor had to come fix it. 

But as for whether the actual restlessness or the trouble focusing got better or stayed the same? I... gosh, I really don't know. I'm honestly not sure. It's so hard to separate what was, you know, my brain being the way it is, versus just the normal, chaotic teenage stuff. 

I mean, high school was just this absolute blur of trying to keep my head above water. I definitely still struggled to pay attention—I remember sitting in Mr. Davis's history class junior year and just staring at the second hand on the clock, feeling like I was going to crawl out of my own skin because he just droned on and on about the Industrial Revolution—but was that feeling *better* than when I was eight? Or was it exactly the same? I really couldn't tell you. 

Maybe I just learned to internalize the fidgeting more so people wouldn't stare? Or maybe I was just so completely exhausted from navigating all the social dynamics... because you know how high school girls can be, every little thing feels like the absolute end of the world, and you're just trying to fit in. So, yeah, I really don't have a clear answer for you on whether the baseline of it actually shifted, or if my life just got so complicated that it sort of masked it. It all just kind of blends together into this one big, overwhelming, messy memory, to be honest.

You mentioned that even activities you enjoy, like the quiet reading evening with your husband, still trigger that restless, jumpy feeling. But I'm curious—are there any activities or situations where you actually *don't* feel that restlessness? For instance, activities that are really engaging or fast-paced or stimulating—do you ever find yourself able to focus or sit still in those situations?

Oh, wow, um... let me really think about that for a second. Because you would think, right? You would absolutely think that if something was just thrilling or moving a mile a minute, that my brain would finally just latch onto it and the rest of my body would settle down. I know some people talk about getting completely sucked into things, like they're in the zone and the rest of the world just melts away. But for me? Honestly, I really can't think of a single situation where that actually happens. I don't think I have anything like that. 

Like, just to give you an example of what I mean... a few months ago, my husband and I went with his sister to one of those escape rooms. You know the ones? Where they lock you in a themed room and you have exactly sixty minutes to solve all these crazy puzzles to get out? It is so fast-paced, and there’s literal adrenaline pumping because the clock is ticking down on this big digital screen on the wall. My sister-in-law, she gets so incredibly laser-focused in those situations, she practically turns to stone while she’s working out a riddle. But me? Even with all that stimulation and pressure, I was still an absolute mess of nervous energy. I couldn't just stand there and focus on one lock. I was pacing all over the small room, picking up a prop, dropping it two seconds later to go look at a painting, talking over my husband while he was trying to read a clue... I was just as jumpy and restless as I am when we're trying to have our quiet reading nights at home. 

Or even if we go to a loud, busy amusement park, or if I'm trying to play a really fast-paced card game with my family... it doesn't matter. The physical feeling of needing to move, that internal motor we talked about, it just doesn't shut off. It’s always humming. I really wish I could give you a great example of an activity where I can just sit still and be totally dialed in without feeling like I need to crawl out of my skin, but I just... I haven't noticed anything that makes that restless feeling go away. It’s just always there, no matter what I'm doing.

Have you ever been formally evaluated or tested for ADHD—attention deficit hyperactivity disorder—either as a child or as an adult? And if so, were you ever prescribed any medications to help with the restlessness or difficulty concentrating?

Oh, no. No, I haven't. And it's actually kind of wild to think about now, because sitting here talking through all of this with you, it feels so incredibly obvious, right? But when I was a kid—this would have been the late eighties and early nineties—nobody really talked about girls having anything like that. It was always the boys, you know? The boys who were literally throwing chairs in the classroom or getting into fights on the playground, those were the ones who got pulled out of class and sent to the school psychologist for testing. 

But me? Like I said earlier, my parents just thought I was a restless kid with too much energy. They figured I was just a handful and that eventually, I'd just magically grow out of it if they kept me busy enough. So there was never any formal testing, no trips to a specialist or anything like that. My mom would have probably been horrified at the very idea of it back then, to be honest. 

And then as an adult... I don't know, you just kind of get used to being the way you are? I just always assumed I was naturally disorganized, or maybe I just wasn't trying hard enough to be a functional adult. You know, you read all these self-help articles and you buy all these expensive organizational systems. Oh my gosh, I have an absolute graveyard of half-used planners in my house right now. Beautiful, expensive, leather-bound planners that I bought swearing *this* was going to be the one that fixed my life, and I used them for exactly three days before losing them under a pile of junk mail on the kitchen counter. I just thought that was a personal failing on my part, a character flaw, not something you actually go to a doctor and get evaluated for. 

So, no, nobody has ever sat me down and given me a formal test or an evaluation. And because of that, no, I've never been prescribed any medications for the restlessness or the focus issues. I've never taken anything at all to help me calm down or concentrate. I've just been white-knuckling it my entire life, trying to manage it on my own with sheer willpower, way too much coffee, and a million sticky notes scattered everywhere. Which, obviously, isn't working out too well for me, hence why I'm finally sitting here talking to you today. But yeah, no testing and no medication ever.

I was always the kid getting up to sharpen a pencil that didn't need sharpening, or asking to go to the bathroom just so I could walk down the hall, or just sort of hovering next to my chair instead of sitting in it. So I guess the feeling of needing to jump out of my skin has always been there, really. It’s just that when you're eight, they just tell you to sit down and stop talking, and now that I'm an adult, it's my kitchen counter that looks like that messy desk, and I don't have a teacher telling me to sit still, I just have this... this awful internal pressure. But yeah, it's definitely not a new thing, it was right there in second and third grade...

inference.note: Ruled out F41.1 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder), F06.8 (Other specified mental disorder due to known physiological condition), and F48.8 (Other specified nonorganic mental disorders). Patient's lifelong history of restlessness, difficulty sustaining attention, impulsivity (blurting out), hyperactivity, organizational difficulties, and forgetfulness starting in elementary school strongly indicates ADHD. The recent worsening is consistent with ADHD becoming more apparent in adulthood when external structure diminishes.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has significant difficulties with attention/focus and task completion, or if the primary issue is primarily motor restlessness and hyperactivity, to help differentiate between predominantly inattentive vs. combined presentation of ADHD
doctor.question: When you're trying to focus on something like reading or paperwork, do you find that your mind wanders or that you have trouble keeping your attention on the task itself, or is it more that your body just won't stay still even though your mind might be willing?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: I can sit down with a planning email or a chapter of a book and start out fine, but after a few minutes I’m staring at the same paragraph and realizing none of it went in.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if my mind wanders and if I have trouble keeping my attention on tasks like reading or paperwork, which directly matches the symptom of difficulty sustaining attention.

patient.answer:
Well, that's the thing, it's really both, but the mind wandering is... it's honestly just as bad as the physical fidgeting, maybe worse, because it feels so out of my control. Like, I’ll tell myself, "Okay, you're going to sit down right now and read this planning email from your sister about the family reunion," or, "You're going to read one chapter of this book for the book club you joined because you thought it would be good for you to get out of the house." And I’ll sit down, and for the first minute or two, I'm doing it. I'm looking at the words, I'm reading the sentences. I start out completely fine. 

But then, it's like a switch flips in my brain, and I don't even realize it's happening at first. I'll be staring right at the screen or the page, and my eyes are moving across the words, so physically I'm doing the action of reading. But my mind is completely gone. I'm thinking about whether I left the porch light on, or remembering a conversation I had three days ago and wondering if I said the wrong thing, or I'm suddenly obsessing over the fact that the dog needs a bath. And then I sort of snap back to reality and realize I've been staring at the exact same paragraph for five minutes, and absolutely none of it went in. Not a single word. 

It’s so incredibly frustrating because I *want* to read it. My mind is willing when I sit down, but it just won't stay there. I have to read the same email three or four times just to understand what time we're supposed to meet for lunch. And with books, I end up having to backtrack pages and pages because I realize I have no idea what just happened in the story. It's like my brain just takes a detour without asking my permission, and it happens every single time I try to focus on something like that. It's exhausting, honestly, just trying to keep my own thoughts on a leash.

inference.note: Added F98.8 (Other specified behavioral and emotional disorders with onset usually in childhood and adolescence) as the patient now reports both lifelong inattention symptoms (mind wandering, difficulty sustaining focus) and hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms (restlessness, inability to sit still, blurting out in childhood). The combination of inattention as a primary feature alongside hyperactivity suggests ADHD, predominantly inattentive or combined presentation. F98.8 is included as differential for other developmental attention/behavioral concerns, though F90.9 (ADHD, unspecified) remains primary candidate given clear developmental history and current functional impairment.

doctor.intent: Distinguish between ADHD (F90.9) and Other Specified Disorder of Infancy, Childhood or Adolescence (F98.8) by determining if the patient has significant impairment in multiple life domains beyond just executive function tasks, or if symptoms are more circumscribed to specific situations like paperwork and reading.
doctor.question: Beyond the difficulty with sitting still and focusing on paperwork or reading, do you find that this restlessness and trouble concentrating affects other areas of your life—like your relationships, your ability to do household chores, or activities you actually enjoy doing?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: The fallout has been that people at home and in my volunteer circles can’t reliably count on me, and I’ve had to step back from some responsibilities because I keep letting things fall through despite trying hard.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about how the symptoms affect different areas of my life, such as relationships, household chores, and enjoyable activities, which directly points to assessing functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. It... it really bleeds into everything. It’s not just the paperwork, it’s honestly my whole life right now, and it breaks my heart to say it, but the fallout has been that people at home just... they can’t reliably count on me. And my husband tries to be understanding, but I see the look on his face when he comes home and the house is a disaster. Like, I’ll start the laundry, right? I'll gather all the baskets, bring them downstairs, but on the way, I notice the hallway mirror is smudged, so I go to the kitchen to get the glass cleaner. But then I see the trash is full, so I pull that out to take to the garage, and then I notice the dog's water bowl is empty so I start scrubbing that out... and three hours later, the laundry is still just sitting in a massive pile in the middle of the stairs and the trash bag is blocking the back door. He just sighs, you know? Because I *am* trying hard. I'm trying so incredibly hard to manage the house like I'm supposed to.

And it’s really spilled over into the things I actually like doing, too. Since I'm not working, I used to be really active in a few volunteer circles—the local PTA, and this community garden project. I loved it, I really did. But I’ve actually had to step back from some of those responsibilities recently because... well, because I keep letting things fall through. I was supposed to organize the spring planting schedule for the garden, which just meant calling a few nurseries and making a simple list for the group. But every time I tried to sit down and do it, I'd get that awful jumpy feeling, or my mind would wander off completely, and I ended up missing the deadline to order the discounted seeds. I let the whole committee down. 

I had sticky notes everywhere, I put reminders in my phone, I even bought a special planner, but it didn't matter. I just kept dropping the ball despite trying my absolute hardest to keep it all together. It got so embarrassing that I finally just emailed the volunteer board and told them I needed to take a step back for personal reasons. But the real reason is just that I know they can't rely on me right now, and I couldn't bear the guilt of messing up their plans again. It’s an awful feeling, knowing you want to help, and you have the time to help, but you just can't trust yourself to actually follow through on any of it...

doctor.intent: Differentiate between ADHD (F90.9) and Other Specified Disorder of Psychological Development (F98.8) by assessing whether the patient experiences significant hyperactivity/restlessness symptoms in situations that don't require sustained attention or sitting still—such as during social gatherings, watching movies, or other leisure activities where movement is naturally permitted.
doctor.question: When you're doing something you really enjoy—like watching a movie, spending time with friends, or doing an activity where you don't have to sit still—do you still feel that same restless, jumpy energy, or does it mainly happen when you're trying to focus on tasks like paperwork?

target_item.name: Quiet_Activity_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: Even when I want a quiet evening reading beside my husband, I end up talking, humming, getting up for little things, or making enough noise that it stops being peaceful.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the restless, jumpy energy occurs during enjoyable or leisure activities like watching a movie, which directly corresponds to the symptom of being unable to engage in leisure activities quietly.

patient.answer:
Oh, I wish it was just the paperwork, I really do. Because you'd think, right? You'd think if it's something relaxing, something I actually *want* to do, my body would just let me enjoy it. But no, it absolutely happens then, too, and it is so incredibly frustrating. 

Like, just the other night, for example. My husband and I, we were trying to just have a nice, quiet evening. He works such long hours, and I just wanted us to have a peaceful night where we sit on the couch together. I had my book—the one for that book club I mentioned earlier—and he was reading the news on his tablet. I even made chamomile tea to try and set this really calm, cozy mood, and I brought out this soft chenille blanket my mother-in-law knitted for us a few years ago. I *want* that quiet evening reading beside my husband so badly. I really do crave that downtime. 

But I sit down, and it’s like my body just completely rejects the quiet. Within five minutes, I'm shifting all my weight around, trying to get comfortable. Then I remember something the neighbor said earlier that day about the trash pickup schedule, so I just blurt it out and start talking, completely breaking the silence. And then I start humming—which I don't even realize I'm doing half the time, it's just this unconscious noise I make, but my husband definitely notices. And then I decide my tea needs a little bit of honey, so I get up to go to the kitchen. Then I sit back down, but my foot is tapping against the coffee table. 

And it just keeps going like that. I end up talking, humming, getting up for all these tiny, insignificant little things, or just generally making enough noise that it completely stops being peaceful. It completely ruins the vibe. And my husband will just kind of sigh and put his tablet down, and I feel terrible because I'm the one who suggested the quiet reading night in the first place! It's like I physically cannot just exist in a quiet, relaxing space, even when it's exactly what I want to be doing, because that jumpy energy just has to get out somehow.

inference.note: Ruled out F98.8. Patient presents with lifelong history of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity across multiple settings (school, home, relationships, leisure activities). Key features include: childhood onset (elementary school), persistent difficulty sustaining attention, constant restlessness and fidgeting, difficulty remaining seated, blurting out/interrupting, organizational problems, forgetfulness, and functional impairment in multiple domains. This is consistent with ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive or combined presentation in adulthood. F98.8 (other specified behavioral and emotional disorders) is less appropriate given the clear ADHD symptom profile and lifelong course.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has difficulty with impulse control and impulsive decision-making, or if symptoms are primarily related to inattention and hyperactivity/restlessness. This helps differentiate ADHD presentations and rule out other conditions.
doctor.question: Beyond the restlessness and trouble focusing, do you find yourself making impulsive decisions or saying things without thinking them through first? For example, do you ever spend money suddenly without planning, interrupt people in conversations, or make snap decisions that you later regret?

target_item.name: Interrupting_Intruding
target_item.manifestation: I care a lot about being respectful, but I still jump into my husband’s conversations or finish people’s thoughts because the response comes out before I’ve made myself wait.
target_item.reason: The doctor specifically asked if I interrupt people in conversations or say things without thinking them through, which directly maps to my symptom of jumping into my husband's conversations and finishing people's thoughts.

patient.answer:
Oh, the interrupting... yes. It is so embarrassing because I really, truly pride myself on being a good listener. Or at least I want to be. I care a lot about being respectful to people, and my parents always taught me how important it is to let others speak, but... I still jump into my husband’s conversations all the time. Or I will just completely finish people’s thoughts for them. 

It happened just this past weekend, actually. My husband was on the phone with his brother, and they were talking about this new car his brother is thinking of buying. Some kind of hybrid, I think, or maybe a small SUV. Anyway, my husband was trying to explain something about the dealership they visited, and I just kept chiming in from the kitchen while I was making lunch. I kept telling him to ask about the warranty, or reminding him to mention the tire package, and he finally had to cover the receiver and give me this exhausted look. 

And it is not just with him, it happens with my friends, too. If someone is telling a story and they pause for even half a second to find a word, I just blurt out the word for them. I think I am being helpful in the moment, or maybe my brain just moves too fast, but the response just comes out before I’ve made myself wait. 

I really do want to let them finish their own sentences. I know exactly how rude it looks. But the words are already out in the air before my brain even registers that I should have kept my mouth shut. It makes me feel so awful because people probably think I just do not care about what they have to say, or that I think my thoughts are more important, but I do care! I really do! It is just this sudden impulse, and I cannot seem to catch it in time, no matter how much I tell myself beforehand to just bite my tongue and listen.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has a history of hyperactivity symptoms in childhood, which would help confirm ADHD diagnosis and rule out other conditions like anxiety or adjustment disorders that typically emerge later
doctor.question: When you were a child in elementary school, beyond the fidgeting and talking out of turn, did teachers or your parents ever describe you as hyperactive or overly energetic? For example, did they say you were always on the go, or that you seemed to have excessive energy compared to other kids your age?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Looking back, this was already part of me in elementary school—I was the girl with a messy desk, forgotten permission slips, and notes from teachers saying I talked out of turn or seemed unable to stay seated.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms during elementary school (prior to age 12), specifically mentioning teachers, talking out of turn, and hyperactivity, which matches the manifestation for onset prior to age 12 years.

patient.answer:
Oh, definitely. Looking back, I mean, it’s so clear to me now that this was already very much a part of me way back in elementary school. It wasn't just a phase or me being a typical kid, you know? 

I was always—and I mean *always*—the girl with the absolute messiest desk in the entire classroom. It was like a black hole in there. I remember in fourth grade, my teacher actually had me stay inside during recess to clean it out because I couldn't find a single assignment, and it was just this avalanche of crumpled up papers, broken crayons, and, of course, all those forgotten permission slips. Oh, the permission slips! My mother used to get so incredibly frustrated with me because I’d almost miss out on field trips to the zoo or the science museum because the slip was just buried at the absolute bottom of my backpack for three weeks, completely crushed under my library books. 

And as for the energy... yes, absolutely. My parents actually kept this whole file folder of my old report cards and progress reports in the hall closet, and it was always the exact same story year after year. They were constantly getting notes from teachers saying that I talked out of turn—which, I guess, goes right along with what I was just saying about interrupting my husband, right? It’s like I haven't changed at all! But the teachers would also specifically write that I seemed completely unable to stay seated. 

They definitely saw me as overly energetic. Like I had a motor inside me that just wouldn't shut off. I would get up to sharpen my pencil five times during a short spelling test, or I'd be kneeling on my chair instead of sitting on it, or I'd just be wandering over to the reading corner when we were supposed to be doing our math worksheets at our desks. My mom used to say I was like a little tornado moving through the house, and the teachers definitely felt that in the classroom, too. It’s actually kind of sad to think about now, because I really wanted to be the good, quiet student who sat perfectly still with her hands folded, but I just... I couldn't keep my body in that little plastic chair. I just had to be moving, and I guess everyone around me definitely noticed it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's symptoms began in childhood (before age 12) and have persisted continuously, which is required for an ADHD diagnosis versus other conditions that might present similarly in adulthood.
doctor.question: When you think back to your childhood—say, between ages 5 and 12—was this restlessness and difficulty concentrating present pretty much all the time during those years, or were there periods where it seemed to go away or get better?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether the symptoms were continuous or episodic during childhood (ages 5 to 12). The symptom profile does not contain an item addressing the course of symptoms during childhood, as 'additional_requirement_1' was already used and 'duration' refers to a recent worsening over the past 1 year and 5 months.

patient.answer:
Hmm, ages five to twelve... let me really think about that. Because, you know, childhood memory can be such a funny thing, especially when you're trying to look back that far and pinpoint exactly how you felt year by year. But honestly? No, I really don't think there was ever a time where it just... stopped. Or even got better. 

I can't remember any sort of magical phase where I suddenly calmed down or could just sit and focus like a normal kid. It feels like it was just this constant, uninterrupted hum in the background of my entire childhood. Like, if I think about kindergarten—I had Mrs. Gable, she was so sweet—I was the one who couldn't stay on my carpet square during storytime without rolling around or bothering the kid next to me. And then you fast forward to, say, third grade, and it was the exact same story, just with harder worksheets and a bigger desk to make a mess of. 

I remember my parents actually thought that maybe I just needed to burn off steam, you know? Like maybe if they just tired me out, the restlessness would go away and I'd be able to pay attention. So they put me in absolutely everything. I did gymnastics, I did swimming lessons at the YMCA, I was in Girl Scouts... oh, I was a Brownie, and we had these meetings in the basement of the Methodist church down the street from our house. And even there, when we were supposed to be sitting at these long folding tables working on our little crafts or listening to the troop leader explain a badge, I was still the one squirming out of my seat, losing my glue stick, completely zoning out while she was giving instructions. 

And it wasn't just during the school year, either! You'd think, oh, it's summer vacation, she doesn't have to concentrate on spelling tests, so maybe the restlessness will take a break. But no, I was just driving my mom crazy at home instead of driving the teachers crazy at school. I'd be pacing around the kitchen, starting a puzzle and abandoning it five minutes later, just constantly bouncing from one thing to the next. 

So, I mean, to answer your question... no, I really don't recall any periods where it faded away. It was just pretty much all the time, every single year, straight through elementary school and right on into middle school. I was just always, always like that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has experienced significant periods of symptom remission or improvement during adolescence or adulthood, which would help clarify if this is lifelong ADHD or if there were developmental changes in symptom presentation.
doctor.question: When you got to middle school and high school, do you remember if the restlessness and trouble focusing got any better, or did it stay pretty much the same as it had been in elementary school?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the progression of symptoms during middle and high school, which is not specifically covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Middle school... wow, that is a whole different era to unpack. You know, going from having just one main teacher in elementary school to suddenly having a different teacher for every single subject... it was such a massive shock to the system. I remember we had these tall, skinny metal lockers, and mine was just... well, it was exactly like my fourth-grade desk, just vertical. I would just shove my winter coat and my gym clothes and all my loose, uncategorized papers in there until the door literally wouldn't latch anymore and the janitor had to come fix it. 

But as for whether the actual restlessness or the trouble focusing got better or stayed the same? I... gosh, I really don't know. I'm honestly not sure. It's so hard to separate what was, you know, my brain being the way it is, versus just the normal, chaotic teenage stuff. 

I mean, high school was just this absolute blur of trying to keep my head above water. I definitely still struggled to pay attention—I remember sitting in Mr. Davis's history class junior year and just staring at the second hand on the clock, feeling like I was going to crawl out of my own skin because he just droned on and on about the Industrial Revolution—but was that feeling *better* than when I was eight? Or was it exactly the same? I really couldn't tell you. 

Maybe I just learned to internalize the fidgeting more so people wouldn't stare? Or maybe I was just so completely exhausted from navigating all the social dynamics... because you know how high school girls can be, every little thing feels like the absolute end of the world, and you're just trying to fit in. So, yeah, I really don't have a clear answer for you on whether the baseline of it actually shifted, or if my life just got so complicated that it sort of masked it. It all just kind of blends together into this one big, overwhelming, messy memory, to be honest.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether symptoms persist across all contexts or improve in stimulating/high-interest environments, to help differentiate ADHD from other conditions
doctor.question: You mentioned that even activities you enjoy, like the quiet reading evening with your husband, still trigger that restless, jumpy feeling. But I'm curious—are there any activities or situations where you actually *don't* feel that restlessness? For instance, activities that are really engaging or fast-paced or stimulating—do you ever find yourself able to focus or sit still in those situations?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about situations where the restlessness and inattention are absent, such as during highly engaging or stimulating activities (hyperfocus or situational variability). There is no specific item in my symptom profile that addresses the absence of symptoms or hyperfocus.

patient.answer:
Oh, wow, um... let me really think about that for a second. Because you would think, right? You would absolutely think that if something was just thrilling or moving a mile a minute, that my brain would finally just latch onto it and the rest of my body would settle down. I know some people talk about getting completely sucked into things, like they're in the zone and the rest of the world just melts away. But for me? Honestly, I really can't think of a single situation where that actually happens. I don't think I have anything like that. 

Like, just to give you an example of what I mean... a few months ago, my husband and I went with his sister to one of those escape rooms. You know the ones? Where they lock you in a themed room and you have exactly sixty minutes to solve all these crazy puzzles to get out? It is so fast-paced, and there’s literal adrenaline pumping because the clock is ticking down on this big digital screen on the wall. My sister-in-law, she gets so incredibly laser-focused in those situations, she practically turns to stone while she’s working out a riddle. But me? Even with all that stimulation and pressure, I was still an absolute mess of nervous energy. I couldn't just stand there and focus on one lock. I was pacing all over the small room, picking up a prop, dropping it two seconds later to go look at a painting, talking over my husband while he was trying to read a clue... I was just as jumpy and restless as I am when we're trying to have our quiet reading nights at home. 

Or even if we go to a loud, busy amusement park, or if I'm trying to play a really fast-paced card game with my family... it doesn't matter. The physical feeling of needing to move, that internal motor we talked about, it just doesn't shut off. It’s always humming. I really wish I could give you a great example of an activity where I can just sit still and be totally dialed in without feeling like I need to crawl out of my skin, but I just... I haven't noticed anything that makes that restless feeling go away. It’s just always there, no matter what I'm doing.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has ever been formally evaluated or diagnosed with ADHD, and whether they have ever taken medication for attention or hyperactivity issues, to clarify if this is a lifelong untreated condition or if there's prior diagnostic history.
doctor.question: Have you ever been formally evaluated or tested for ADHD—attention deficit hyperactivity disorder—either as a child or as an adult? And if so, were you ever prescribed any medications to help with the restlessness or difficulty concentrating?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about previous formal evaluations, testing, or medication for ADHD, which is not covered by the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, no. No, I haven't. And it's actually kind of wild to think about now, because sitting here talking through all of this with you, it feels so incredibly obvious, right? But when I was a kid—this would have been the late eighties and early nineties—nobody really talked about girls having anything like that. It was always the boys, you know? The boys who were literally throwing chairs in the classroom or getting into fights on the playground, those were the ones who got pulled out of class and sent to the school psychologist for testing. 

But me? Like I said earlier, my parents just thought I was a restless kid with too much energy. They figured I was just a handful and that eventually, I'd just magically grow out of it if they kept me busy enough. So there was never any formal testing, no trips to a specialist or anything like that. My mom would have probably been horrified at the very idea of it back then, to be honest. 

And then as an adult... I don't know, you just kind of get used to being the way you are? I just always assumed I was naturally disorganized, or maybe I just wasn't trying hard enough to be a functional adult. You know, you read all these self-help articles and you buy all these expensive organizational systems. Oh my gosh, I have an absolute graveyard of half-used planners in my house right now. Beautiful, expensive, leather-bound planners that I bought swearing *this* was going to be the one that fixed my life, and I used them for exactly three days before losing them under a pile of junk mail on the kitchen counter. I just thought that was a personal failing on my part, a character flaw, not something you actually go to a doctor and get evaluated for. 

So, no, nobody has ever sat me down and given me a formal test or an evaluation. And because of that, no, I've never been prescribed any medications for the restlessness or the focus issues. I've never taken anything at all to help me calm down or concentrate. I've just been white-knuckling it my entire life, trying to manage it on my own with sheer willpower, way too much coffee, and a million sticky notes scattered everywhere. Which, obviously, isn't working out too well for me, hence why I'm finally sitting here talking to you today. But yeah, no testing and no medication ever.

Current symptoms include persistent difficulty sustaining attention (mind wandering during reading/paperwork despite willingness), pervasive restlessness and motor hyperactivity (inability to sit still, constant fidgeting, foot tapping, getting up frequently), impulsivity (interrupting, blurting out comments, talking out of turn), and significant functional impairment across multiple domains (household management, volunteer work, relationships). Symptoms are present across diverse contexts (work, home, leisure) and have persisted throughout life without remission periods. No prior formal evaluation or medication trial. Meets criteria for ADHD, Combined Presentation (F90.2) or Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Presentation (F90.1), though insufficient detail on inattention alone suggests F90.9 (ADHD, unspecified) as most conservative coding given lack of formal diagnostic assessment.
